title: Fight band at the arena, Triangle Band and the Palace vaudeville job
summary: He played ballyhoo and fights with Dan Hughes and George Brunies, then the Triangle Band, and Joe Fulco got him a vaudeville job where two musicians taught him to read.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: That's a one-eyed trumpet? Yeah. That's right.

So, when I went to work there, who was playing padcom with Dan Hughes was George and Brunus. Oh, yeah. So, we used to play the fight and all that, like the jungle, the arena, you know what I mean? Used to be the Tulane arena. Used to be the Tulane arena. So, all these musicians. Well, we used to ballet-hoo all day long. And, uh, time to get in the fight. Well, you'd have about 40 musicians with the trombones for fitting in the, you know, getting in the band just to get in the fight, to see the fight, see? So, I finally went there for, oh, for about a year or something like that. Then I went with the Triangle Band, which was about playing with Sato Majada, the other thing again?
That used to be with the police band. Yeah, that's right. You read Majada's brother. Yeah, that's right. So...
He died, didn't he? Yeah, he died. Yeah. Yeah. So then I played with him quite a while.

But, uh, we used to, uh, bounty-hoo on Dauphin Street. So, Joe Fulco called me on the side. He says, hey boy, I had to give you a job. I said, what? He says, to play vaudeville. I said, well, I'm not that good. I said, you know, I can't read music that good to play vaudeville, see? He says, I'll teach you. Yeah, well, Sidney Wilson, I don't know if you know the piano player Sidney Wilson? No, I don't know him. He was a trombone player too. Leo Brookhoven, Trappertone. So those two guys really helped me, you know, how to read and all that stuff. And, uh, I played at theater for quite a while. Then I got more damn offers to go to New York, you know, like Lanning, and all these guys sent me telegrams, offered me a lot of money to leave there. We had all these vaudeville entertainers like a, see, they played a circuit, see, and they said, man, you want to hear a trombone play? I'm bragging about myself there. He says, go into New Orleans. I said, I want to hear a kid that plays trombone, he plays good. But I used to stand up and play solos all the time. You know, like I said, at that time I didn't have no competition. They had just about four or five cromwell players that, you know, I knew how to play around here.
